name: Dr. Kimberly's residence
aka: Dr. Kimberly's house east of the Lake House

documented_range.note: NEITHER END IS DATED BY A SOURCE. THE START IS THE FIRST DAY THE ATTESTED YEAR PERMITS, not a date anybody gives - the same convention, for the same reason, that lake_house_construction's own range opens on. The one sighting is the morning of 26 August 1835, eight weeks AFTER the scene date, and a range opening there would put this house outside the scene it is attested in. What carries it back is an argument about the household and not about the building: Kimberly's partnership with Pruyne is in the town from 1832-33 by this project's own committed household record, the drug store on South Water Street is a going concern in the 1835 newspapers, and nothing in Bonnell's sentence reads as a house eight weeks old. That is an inference and it is graded as one. THE END IS THE HONEST YEAR BOUND: nothing reached says when this house came down, was sold or was replaced, and the 1843 and 1844 directories that print Kimberly do not print a dwelling for him. BONNELL'S WALK IS THE ONLY SOURCE THIS PROJECT HAS REACHED THAT DESCRIBES THE GROUND EAST OF THE LAKE HOUSE BUILDING SITE, AND IT IS ONE SENTENCE LONG. J. D. Bonnell, writing to the Chicago Times on 15 March 1876 and quoted by Andreas (History of Chicago vol. 1, printed pages 136-137), describes the morning after he arrived: "Passing east, toward the mouth of the river, was the Lake House in course of construction, east of which was the residence of Dr. Kimball, who was a partner of Mr. Pruyne in a drug store on South Water Street. Mr. Pruyne was State Senator." THE MAN IS IDENTIFIED THREE WAYS OVER AND THE SPELLING IS BONNELL'S OR HIS TYPESETTER'S. "Dr. Kimball" is Dr Edmund Stoughton Kimberly: a doctor, Peter Pruyne's partner, and a druggist on South Water Street are three attributes and this project already holds all three on one household - data/residents/households/hh_pruyne_kimberly.json, "The Pruyne and Kimberly partnership household", headed by Peter Pruyne, recorded trade druggist, whose own arrival note quotes Moses and Kirkland naming "Dr. E. S. Kimberly ... of Vermont". Pruyne's senatorship is the fourth check and it is right: he sat for this district. No other Kimball or Kimberly in the identity master is a physician or Pruyne's partner. THE DATE IS EIGHT WEEKS LATE AND THE CARRY BACK IS THE INFERENCE. The letter dates the arrival to 25 August 1835, so the walk is the morning of the 26th - eight weeks after the scene date. The same letter's "forty years ago" implies 1836 and Andreas's lead-in says Bonnell "came to Chicago in 1837"; the 1837 reading is ruled out by the letter's own content, since the Lake House was open by the autumn of 1836, and between 1835 and 1836 this project prefers the letter's explicit date, which is the ruling already committed on data/structures/lake_house_construction.json. See docs/RESEARCH/north_bank_east_end_neighbours.md.

placement.position_note: PLACED AGAINST ONE BUILDING AND NOT AGAINST THE GROUND, AND THE BUILDING IT IS PLACED AGAINST IS ITSELF RECONSTRUCTED. The evidence is the word "east": "the Lake House in course of construction, east of which was the residence of Dr. Kimball". No source gives this house a street, a corner, a lot or a distance. METHOD: the west face is set 12.0 m east of lake_house_construction's committed east face, and the north face on the same line as the Lake House's own north face, so the two front the same frontage with a yard between them. THE 12.0 m AND THE SHARED FRONT LINE ARE BOTH INVENTED. This position therefore inherits every uncertainty the Lake House's carries and adds one of its own: the Lake House's own note records that which side of Rush Street its block is on is not documented at all and that if the east side is wrong the building belongs about 110 m west, and that this project's georeference of that corner carries about 20 m of working uncertainty. If the Lake House moves, this house moves with it, which is the honest consequence of a placement whose whole content is "east of". WORKING UNCERTAINTY about 110 m, governed by the side of Rush Street and not by the survey. Facade bearing 0, due north onto Michigan Street, follows the Lake House, which is the one building on this frontage a source orients; nothing states this one's. The ground here is the e1834_harbor_cut heightfield at about +1.51 m above the summer-1835 water surface - traced ground - so the record declares no ground contact of its own. ONE DISAGREEMENT THIS POSITION DOES NOT RESOLVE, and it is not this record's to resolve: the committed michigan_north centreline runs at local N 390.0 here, which puts this frontage 21.6 m back from the street corridor's south edge rather than on it. The Lake House stands at the same setback for the same reason - its frontage was fitted to the modern Hubbard/Rush corner and not to the committed street - and moving either building onto the committed line is a question about michigan_north's geometry, filed rather than answered here.
placement.symbolic_location: North side of the river in Kinzie's Addition, on the Michigan Street frontage east of the Lake House building site (today the south side of East Hubbard Street east of North Rush Street), fronting north onto Michigan Street.

footprint.note: PLACEHOLDER - NO DIMENSION IS ATTESTED. 11.0 x 8.0 m is about 36 x 26 ft, an eaves-front house of two rooms and a passage on the front range. Every number is invented. The only thing bounding the size is who lived here: Bonnell calls it a "residence" rather than a house or a cabin, and its occupant is a physician and half of a South Water Street drug firm, so the house is given the frontage of a professional man's dwelling and not a labourer's cabin. That is an argument about a trade and not a measurement. It is deliberately smaller than the frame houses this project has raised on stated dimensions, because nothing here is stated at all.

construction.note: NOT ATTESTED, AND THE ALTERNATIVE WAS LOG. Bonnell says nothing about this building's fabric. Chicago in 1835 is three years into balloon framing - invented here in 1833 at St Mary's church, which this project already records - and the north bank east end is new ground being built on by men with money, so a frame house is the reconstruction and a braced frame or a log house are the refused alternatives. Recorded as reconstructed, not inferred: there is no evidence about THIS building to reason from.

stories.note: Not attested. The story-and-a-half is the characteristic form of these years and this archetype's own default; nothing about this house is stated, so it takes it.

wall_height_m.note: No figure is attested. 3.4 m is the low end of this archetype's band for a story-and-a-half - a full storey of the one attested Chicago ceiling height, the Green Tree's seven and a half feet, plus floor structure and the knee wall the half storey's chambers stand on. Invented for this building, and taken low because nothing here is stated at all.

roof_type.note: Not attested. Gable is the near-universal roof form for a frame dwelling of this type, period and region, and it is what the half storey's gable-end chambers require.

chimneys.note: Not attested. Two stacks is the hall-and-parlour arrangement - a hearth to each of the two front rooms - and is invented for this house. The archetype decides where they stand (L26).

siding_exposure_m.note: INVENTED WITHIN A STOCK SET, NOT DERIVED. No source states the exposed face of any Chicago building's siding. The value is one of four period mill sidings — 4.5, 5, 5.5 or 6 in to the weather; this record wears 4.5 in — dealt by tools/deal_siding_stock.py: keyed to the phase's construction season, because buildings sided from the same season's shipments of St Joseph sawn lumber tend toward one stock, then advanced so no frame building within 60 m shares this one's. The separation is the surface variety T-0049 reconstructs, not a claim about 1835. docs/LIBERTIES.md L148 owns the invention.

function.note: "east of which was the residence of Dr. Kimball" - Bonnell names the use in the same clause as the building. It is the one attribute of this structure a source states outright.

occupants.value: Dr Edmund Stoughton Kimberly, physician, and a partner in the drug store on South Water Street
occupants.note: THE OCCUPANT IS ATTESTED AND, SINCE T-2140, SO IS THE HOUSEHOLD THAT CARRIES HIM. Bonnell names the man and gives him this building, which is as direct as this corpus gets. Until T-2140 the household record that held him was hh_pruyne_kimberly, a PARTNERSHIP household headed by Peter Pruyne and banded to the south division on the evidence of the store, and seating that household here would have moved Pruyne across the river on a sentence about Kimberly - so this roof named its occupant and claimed no household. T-2140 split the partnership: Kimberly heads hh_kimberly_edmund_s, whose lives_at names this roof, and Pruyne stays on hh_pruyne_kimberly with the store. AND THE PARTNER IS NAMED IN THIS NOTE AND NOT IN THE VALUE, WHICH IS NOT squeamishness: tools/compile_register.py matches a firm onto a committed roof on its partners' surnames read out of the `occupants` line, so writing Peter Pruyne into the occupants of Kimberly's HOUSE moved P. Pruyne & Co.'s premises off pruyne_kimball_drugstore and onto this roof - the drug store on South Water Street relocated to a dwelling on the north bank by a sentence about somebody else. The occupants line says who occupied the building; the partnership is a fact about the man and is recorded here and in the research note.

land_owner.value: The ground was entered by Robert A Kenzie, 7 May 1831
land_owner.note: KINZIE'S ADDITION. The north fraction of section 10 is the section north of the river, which is why the register prints 102.29 acres and not a quarter's 160. It is resolved as the section's own grid box clipped to the committed north bank of the main stem (`e1834_harbor_cut/shoreline.geojson`), so no boundary here is authored. The two rows the register carries for it — one plain, one with the school-section marker — are the same entry printed twice. THE REGISTER SPELLS THE PURCHASER MORE THAN ONE WAY for this same tract — Robert A Kenzie; Robert A Kinzie — and the spellings are carried rather than merged, which is the land_sales crosswalk's standing rule: tract agreement is where two spellings MIGHT be one man and is never proof that they are. THE MARGIN IS 53 m: this footprint stands that far inside the tract's nearest boundary, which is more than twice the working horizontal uncertainty of anything traced off the 1834 sheets (about 20 m), so the assignment survives the error the construction carries. WHAT THIS ROW CLAIMS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. It claims that the tract the Illinois State Archives' land-sale register describes contains this structure's committed position — the patent for this ground was ENTERED by this man on this date. It does not claim he still held the ground on 1 July 1835, that he lived here, or that he ever stood on it: a sale is a transaction, and the register's only column about residence names a county. THE SECTION LINES ARE CONSTRUCTED, NOT TRACED (L219): the grid is carried from the single PLSS corner at State & Madison, on the plat's own east-west bearing, in nominal one-mile squares.

residents.name: The Kimberly household
residents.why: SEATED BY T-2140 IN THE HOUSE BONNELL GIVES HIM. J. D. Bonnell's letter of 1876, quoted by Andreas (vol. 1, printed pages 136-137): "east of which [the Lake House] was the residence of Dr. Kimball, who was a partner of Mr. Pruyne in a drug store on South Water Street." A doctor, Pruyne's partner, and a druggist on South Water Street identify this man three ways over; data/structures/kimberly_residence.json raised the building on that sentence and named him its occupant, and refused to write the household link while he shared a record with Pruyne, because seating the partnership there would have carried Pruyne across the river on a sentence about Kimberly. With the two men on two records the link is written from this side, which is the direction the evidence runs in. GRADED AT THE INFERENCE, NOT THE SENTENCE: the walk is the morning of 26 August 1835, eight weeks after the scene date, and the carry back to 1 July is the inference. A LATER DIRECTORY AGREES AND IS NOT LEANED ON: Fergus's 1839 directory prints 'Kimberly, Dr. Edmund S., res. N. Water st next Lake House' (f1839_e0850) - the same spot four years on, which corroborates the house and dates nothing in 1835. The record names a committed structure; the roof is the evidence's own limit and nothing narrower is claimed. COPIED FROM THE SINGULAR `lives_at` AND ITS RECONCILIATION ROW `hh_kimberly_edmund_s#lives_at`, changing no value, confidence or source. That field names the place as of 1 July 1835 and dates neither end of the relationship, so this row is `undated` rather than borrowing the scene date as a start (T-1273)

persons.name: Dr Edmund Stoughton Kimberly
persons.note: T-0478 adds exact birth data and independent biography: born April 7, 1803 at Troy, New York; Union College graduate; medical training in New York; married Marie Theresa Ellis May 16, 1829; moved to Chicago in 1832. He was clerk of the August 5, 1833 incorporation meeting and one of the first town trustees. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 2 times: Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Kimberly, Edmund S.” (tax_1833_057, line 109); Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Kimberly, Dr. E. S.” (poll_1834_063, line 232). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Kimberly' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json). THE 1840 FEDERAL CENSUS — A HEAD FIVE YEARS AFTER THE SCENE, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1840 federal census of Chicago, read line by line off the left sheets in this repository, carries 1 head of this name — “Ed. Kimberley” (33S7-9YYJ-99F, printed page 234, line 3). This project has ruled the head a CANDIDATE and no more: the name agrees and is unique on both sides, but nothing independent of the name was found. A candidate is not an identity — nothing is asserted from it, no household of 1840 is carried back, and the ruling is recorded so that a reader can see it was made rather than missed. Under the rule that decided it (L6b reached_through_a_card_merge_caps_at_candidate), by the crosswalk's own ladder (data/research/census_1840/resident_crosswalk.json). LATER EVIDENCE ONLY. The ratified grading ladder binds: an 1839 or 1840 appearance alone is never an 1835 resident, and 1840 household composition is never back-projected to the 1835-07-01 scene. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and an 1840 head is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 4 times, as “KIMBERLEY EDMUND S”, “KIMBERLY EDMUND S”, “KIMBERLY E S”, 1833-10-25 to 1836-09-05: 1 federal land entry — E2SE sec 32 T39N R14E and 2 lots in the platted town — lot 5 of block 1 in the town the register codes CHI (L5BL1CHI, as printed); lot 9 of block 48 in the town the register codes CHIOTV (L9BL48CHIOTV, as printed) and 1 parcel of the school section — lot 6 of block 119 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), 80.00 acres stated in all, for $5042.00 (ls0263, ls0479, ls1281, ls1282). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $4300.00 to the money. This project does not expand the register's town codes, so which addition a lot stands in is carried as the code and not as a name. It is still a purchase and it still places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: KIMBERLEY EDMUND S matches Dr Edmund Stoughton Kimberly: the forename names Dr Edmund Stoughton Kimberly of the 1 person of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. The surname reaches him through a ruled card merge and not off his card: the town held kimberley_ed until data/residents/card_merge_rulings.json folded it onto this person, and the register's spelling is the one that card carried. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

persons.name: Marie Theresa Ellis Kimberly
persons.note: NAMED AND DATED IN THE SOURCE - the history of medicine in Chicago gives Dr Edmund Stoughton Kimberly's marriage as 'married Marie Theresa Ellis May 16, 1829', three years before he came to Chicago and six before the scene date. The printed line runs her name into the month; 'May' is the month and not a surname. WHAT THE SOURCE DOES NOT SAY: it does not say she came west with him, and nothing in this project places her at Chicago on 1 July 1835. She is written because a named wife of a named head is the person this layer exists to record, and the presence on the day is the reconstruction, not the marriage. Her household was split out of the Pruyne-Kimberly partnership by T-2140 and stands on Bonnell's 'residence of Dr. Kimball' east of the Lake House; she is seated there because her husband is, and no source puts her in that house. No age, no occupation and no arrival is claimed for her.

residents.research_note: SPLIT OUT OF THE PRUYNE AND KIMBERLY PARTNERSHIP HOUSEHOLD BY T-2140. That record grouped two men because they opened a drug store together, and said in its own words that nothing put them under one roof and that it should not be given a dwelling until the two were separated. Bonnell's walk then put one of them in a house on the north bank east of the Lake House and the other's store on South Water Street, so the two are two households: Peter Pruyne stays on hh_pruyne_kimberly with the store, and Dr Kimberly heads this one, seated where Bonnell saw him. NOTHING ON THE MAN WAS RE-READ: his card moved across whole, every reading on it with the grade it already held, and only his relationship changed - from the partnership's `partner` to this household's `head`. A NAME COLLISION KEPT SEPARATE, AS BEFORE: the W. Kimball who advertised dry goods at South Water and Clark in the Democrat of 26 November 1833 is a different trade and a different man, with his own household.

WHAT IS INVENTED, PLAINLY: the distance east of the Lake House, the frontage and depth, the storey and a half, the wall height, the roof, both chimneys, the frame construction and the bearing. WHAT IS ATTESTED: that the building existed, that it was a residence, that it stood east of the Lake House, and who lived in it. WHAT WOULD UPGRADE THIS RECORD: the Kinzie's Addition conveyances, which would give the lot and therefore the maximum plan and would settle which side of Rush Street the Lake House block is on; the Chicago American or the Chicago Democrat for 1835-36, which carried building notices; or anything that gives Kimberly a street or a corner.
